e: Routers forward traffic based on the Layer 3 destination IP address; switches forward based on the Layer 2 MAC address (Layer 3 switches are an exception)
d: IP addresses on a router are configured per physical interface (or subinterface), not per VLAN. Routers also have no MAC address table.

e: An auxiliary port, configured under line aux 0, that can be connected to an external modem or phone line for emergency out-of-band access
d: Faster interfaces are typically used for this purpose in modern networks instead.

e: show ip interface brief gives a brief summary; show protocols and show interfaces give longer summaries; show ip interface gives full status
d: Routers don't support "show interfaces status" — that's switch-only.

e: Local (route to a configured interface's own IP) · Connected (route to an interface's subnet) · Static (manually defined) · Dynamic (learned via a routing protocol) · Default/gateway of last resort (used when nothing else matches)

t: Static route — next-hop vs outbound interface
e: ip route subnet mask nexthop specifies the next router's IP; ip route subnet mask interface specifies the outbound interface directly (shown as "directly connected")
d: The next-hop option is generally preferred, but the interface option is useful when the next-hop IP might change, e.g. it's assigned via DHCP.

e: IOS checks that the outbound interface is up, or that it has a route to the specified next-hop IP, before adding a static route
d: If the check fails the route isn't added at all, even once the issue is fixed later — add the permanent keyword to override this.

e: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 nexthop/interface
d: Acts as a catch-all "last resort" route, typically sending traffic destined for the Internet out of the internal network.

e: When multiple routes match a destination, the one with the longest (most specific) prefix is used
d: E.g. a /24 route to a destination wins over a matching /16 route, even though both technically match.

e: When multiple routes exist to the exact same network and prefix, the one with the lowest Administrative Distance (0-255) is installed
d: The others are kept in their routing protocol's own database in case the preferred route is later removed.

e: Connected 0 · Static 1 · EIGRP summary 5 · eBGP 20 · Internal EIGRP 90 · IGRP 100 · OSPF 110 · IS-IS 115 · RIP 120 · External EIGRP 170 · iBGP 200 · DHCP default gateway 254 · Unknown 255
A static route configured with a higher-than-default Administrative Distance so a dynamic route is preferred over it
d: Used to provide a backup path (often over a lower-bandwidth link) that only takes over once the dynamic route disappears from the routing table.

e: When routes tie on both destination and Administrative Distance, the one with the best metric (the routing protocol's own notion of "best path") is installed
d: RIP uses hop count; EIGRP uses "metric"; OSPF uses "cost" — both EIGRP and OSPF automatically factor in link bandwidth, unlike RIP.

e: Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) load-balances traffic when a router learns multiple routes with identical Administrative Distance and metric
d: EIGRP is the exception that can also do Unequal Cost Multi-Path load balancing if configured.
An OSPF-learned route (O) to 10.2.2.0/30 with Administrative Distance 110 and metric 128, next-hop 10.2.2.5, outbound via Serial0/0/1.

e: Each VLAN/IP subnet gets its own dedicated physical router interface
d: Rarely used in practice — you run out of router interfaces as VLANs grow, and routed traffic must physically travel to and from the router over Ethernet cabling.

e: Multiple VLANs are trunked to a single router interface, with each VLAN routed via its own subinterface
d: Subinterfaces are named e.g. Gi0/0.10 and each needs encapsulation dot1q n (add the native keyword for the native VLAN) plus its own IP address.

e: A switch that supports both Layer 2 frame forwarding and Layer 3 IP routing, using either SVI-based routing or routed physical ports (no switchport)
d: Requires sdm prefer lanbase-routing (on some models) plus ip routing enabled globally. This is the most common approach in modern networks since routing happens across the switch backbone instead of over external cabling.

e: Requires both a route to the pinged host and a route back from that host to you
d: Entering "ping" with no parameters prompts for all parameters including source IP — useful for reverse route testing. Can use hostnames if a DNS server is configured.

e: Shows every hop to a destination by manipulating a test packet's TTL, starting at 1 and incrementing until the destination is reached
d: IOS traceroute encapsulates UDP inside IP packets, while most other operating systems use ICMP echo requests — so the two can be differently affected by security rules on the path.

e: ssh -l username address
d: Initiates an outbound SSH session from EXEC mode.
